slides.title: Testing of liver enzymes
bullets: General topics in clinical biochemistry
Practical session — 6 h

slides.title: Lesson outline
bullets: Tests: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT); Aspartate aminotransferase (AST); Alkaline phosphatase (ALP); Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
Conditions: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD); Viral hepatitis B
Tables and algorithms: Cytolysis (hepatocellular injury); Cholestasis; Hepatocellular failure (synthetic function); De Ritis ratio (AST/ALT)
Practice: Q&A: 12 + 3

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used in routine screening of liver health and to help diagnose or monitor liver problems, usually as part of a liver function panel. Some liver diseases raise ALT before symptoms appear, so the test may help detect them early.

Ordered when there are symptoms of liver damage (for example jaundice, dark urine or light-colored stool, abdominal swelling or pain, frequent itching) or a high risk of liver damage: family history of liver disease, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, or hepatitis or exposure to it.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: ALT is usually measured together with AST in a liver function panel. Because ALT is found mostly in the liver, it checks more specifically for liver damage.
Physiology: ALT (alanine transaminase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, and its blood level is usually low. When liver cells are damaged, they release ALT into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
cols: Possible causes of liver damage with a high ALT: hepatitis, infection, cirrhosis, liver cancer, other liver diseases, a lack of blood flow to the liver, certain medicines (such as cholesterol or pain medicines) and poisons.
Low ALT is not common and may lead to further testing. Possible causes include vitamin B6 deficiency and chronic kidney disease.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
cols: Cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern: ALT and AST are raised disproportionately to alkaline phosphatase. It points to liver-cell injury; the work-up looks for viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, alcohol, medicines and other causes.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALT is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: A high ALT does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Age, sex, weight, certain medicines and dietary supplements, intense exercise and the phase of the menstrual cycle can affect the result.
Limitations: ALT is interpreted together with the other liver tests. It may help tell acute from chronic liver problems, but the ALT level does not reflect how much of the liver is damaged.

slides.title: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)
bullets: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

The liver’s synthetic function (hepatocellular failure pattern) is judged not by enzymes but by proteins the liver makes: albumin and prothrombin time (PT/INR); bilirubin also reflects the liver’s clearing work. A high ALT by itself does not mean liver failure.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Part of routine screening of liver health; helps diagnose or monitor liver problems and may help diagnose other conditions. It may be ordered alone but is often part of a liver function panel.

Ordered at routine checkups, to monitor treatment of a liver problem, with symptoms of liver damage (such as jaundice, nausea, abdominal swelling or pain, dark urine), or without symptoms when liver disease risk is higher (family history, alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, medicines that can harm the liver, hepatitis or exposure to it).

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: AST (aspartate aminotransferase) is an enzyme found mainly in the liver, but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues. Its blood level is usually low; when the liver or other AST-containing cells are damaged, AST is released into the blood.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
cols: High AST may be due to liver disease or other liver problems. Other possible causes: hepatitis, cirrhosis, mononucleosis, heart procedures or problems, pancreatitis, hemochromatosis (too much iron), deep burns, seizures, use of drugs toxic to the liver (especially alcohol) and surgery.
Low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
cols: ALT is often ordered together with AST. High AST and/or ALT may mean some type of liver damage.
AST rising with ALT out of proportion to alkaline phosphatase indicates a cytolytic (hepatocellular) pattern; if ALP predominates, a cholestatic pattern.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so. AST is usually ordered with other blood tests, which often require fasting for up to 12 hours.
Interferences: A result outside the normal range does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Pregnancy, exercise, certain medicines, age and sex can affect the result.

Limitations: When liver test results are abnormal, the provider compares all the measured substances to look for patterns that suggest different types of liver conditions. Liver function tests alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

slides.title: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)
bullets: The De Ritis ratio is AST/ALT. Classically it is usually above 2 in alcoholic liver disease and below 1 in chronic viral hepatitis and chronic cholestasis; in non-alcoholic liver disease a ratio above 1 may suggest cirrhosis. With cirrhosis the ratio separates alcoholic from non-alcoholic causes less well. AST is also found in heart and muscle, so the ratio is meaningful only for liver conditions.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to screen for or help diagnose liver and bone diseases and to help diagnose or monitor other conditions. Often done with a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) or liver function tests, or when there are symptoms of liver damage or a bone disorder (bone pain, joint inflammation, unusually shaped or enlarged bones, broken bones).
Physiology: ALP is an enzyme present in all body tissues, with higher amounts in the liver, bile ducts and bones. Each part of the body makes a different type of ALP.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
cols: High ALP from the liver may be a sign of bile duct blockage, cirrhosis, hepatitis or mononucleosis (which can sometimes cause swelling in the liver).
If ALP is high and liver tests are normal, a bone disorder such as Paget's disease of bone is possible.

Low ALP is less common. Possible causes: zinc deficiency, protein deficiency, malnutrition, pernicious anemia, thyroid disease, Wilson disease and hypophosphatasia (a rare genetic disease affecting bones and teeth).

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
cols: Moderately high ALP may occur with many conditions, including Hodgkin lymphoma, heart failure and certain infections; a high ALP may also occur without a condition that needs treatment.
Cholestatic pattern: alkaline phosphatase is raised out of proportion to ALT and AST.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
cols: A raised GGT supports a liver source. If bilirubin rises too, bile-duct obstruction is considered.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; some may need to be paused, but only on the provider's advice. Because ALP is usually ordered with other blood tests, fasting for several hours is often required.

Interferences: Pregnancy can raise ALP, and children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing. Birth control pills and some medicines may lower ALP while others raise it, and a fatty meal before the test may cause a small increase.

slides.title: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
bullets: Limitations: The ALP test alone cannot tell which tissue the ALP comes from, so other tests are usually needed. An ALP isoenzyme test can show its source (not available everywhere); if liver function tests are also high, the ALP is likely of liver origin.

Abnormal liver test results don't always mean a liver problem: high ALP, for example, can be a sign of bone disease as well as liver disease. The provider also considers symptoms, medical history, liver disease risk and medicines taken.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood

What it is used for: Used to help diagnose liver disease, to tell liver disease from a bone disorder, to check for bile duct blockage, and to screen for or monitor alcohol use disorder. Drinking alcohol raises GGT, and most people with alcohol use disorder have high GGT.
Usually done with or after other liver tests, most often ALP. Both GGT and ALP may rise in diseases of the liver and bile ducts, but only ALP rises in bone disease.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
slides.eyebrow: Liver · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: GGT is an enzyme found throughout the body but mainly in the liver. If the liver or bile ducts are damaged, GGT may leak into the bloodstream.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
cols: High GGT may be a sign of liver damage. Possible causes include hepatitis, cirrhosis, alcohol use disorder, pancreatitis, diabetes, heart failure and medicine side effects. The result cannot show which condition is responsible, but usually the higher the GGT, the more liver damage.
A low or normal GGT means liver disease is unlikely.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
cols: Compared with ALP: high ALP with high GGT points to a liver disorder rather than a bone disorder, while high ALP with low or normal GGT makes a bone disorder more likely.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
bullets: Pre-analytics: Ask the provider about specific instructions; fasting for a set time before the test may be requested.
Interferences: Results may be affected by certain medicines or supplements, drinking alcohol and smoking cigarettes. GGT levels go down after meals.

Limitations: GGT cannot identify the specific cause of liver disease; it only indicates that the liver is being damaged. The provider interprets it with symptoms, medical history and other blood tests.

slides.title: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
bullets: Among liver laboratory patterns GGT belongs to the cholestatic group: rising with ALP supports a hepatobiliary cause, while a high ALP with normal GGT supports bone. GGT also rises with alcohol and some medicines, so alone it does not prove cholestasis.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
bullets: Fat builds up in the liver. Overweight, insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides and metabolic syndrome raise the risk. Diagnosis uses blood tests, imaging and sometimes biopsy; alcohol intake and other causes of liver fat are also assessed.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
rows: Raised ALT and AST may lead the clinician to suspect MASLD.
Calculated from routine blood results; help identify or rule out advanced liver fibrosis.
Tests for other causes of raised liver enzymes
Additional blood tests for other conditions that can raise liver enzymes.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
rows: ALT/AST ↑ + risk factors (obesity, type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides)
MASLD is possible — imaging and exclusion of other causes are needed.
Advanced fibrosis is possible — elastography; biopsy is sometimes recommended.

slides.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)
bullets: Routine imaging shows liver fat but not inflammation or fibrosis. Only a biopsy can prove MASH.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
bullets: CDC recommends screening all adults 18 and older at least once with a triple panel (HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc), and testing for HBsAg in every pregnancy. Total anti-HBc is required to diagnose infection; the other markers show the type of infection and immunity.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
rows: Indicates infectiousness (may be transiently positive within 30 days after a vaccine dose).
Indicates recovery and immunity, or successful vaccination.
Previous or ongoing infection of undefined timing; lasts for life and is absent after vaccination alone.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
rows: Recent infection (within about 6 months); ordered only when acute infection is a concern.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
rows: Acute infection is likely — link to care.
Chronic infection is likely — link to care.
Resolved infection; counsel on reactivation risk.

slides.title: Viral hepatitis B
rows: Isolated anti-HBc: resolved infection with waned anti-HBs, occult infection, a false positive, or a mutant HBsAg missed by the assay — needs further evaluation.

slides.title: Cytolysis (hepatocellular injury)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: Markers: ALT and AST ↑ out of proportion to ALP
Meaning: Liver-cell injury: hepatitis, fatty liver, alcohol, medicines

slides.title: Cholestasis
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: Markers: ALP ↑ out of proportion to ALT/AST; GGT ↑ (liver source); direct bilirubin often ↑
Meaning: Impaired bile flow; ALP ↑ with normal GGT — think of bone

slides.title: Hepatocellular failure (synthetic function)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: Markers: Albumin ↓, prolonged prothrombin time (PT/INR), bilirubin ↑
Meaning: The liver makes too little protein and clotting factors; a high ALT alone does not mean this

slides.title: De Ritis ratio (AST/ALT)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Liver laboratory patterns
bullets: > 2: Usually alcoholic liver disease
< 1: Chronic viral hepatitis, chronic cholestasis
> 1 (non-alcoholic disease): May suggest cirrhosis
AST is also in heart and muscle — the ratio only makes sense for liver conditions.

slides.title: A patient's ALT is markedly high. What does the ALT level itself tell you about how much of the liver is damaged?
options: The higher the ALT, the larger the share of the liver that has been damaged
Nothing reliable — the ALT level is not related to the extent of damage
A high ALT confirms that cirrhosis is the cause of the damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the ALT level does not reflect the extent of damage; it is interpreted together with the other liver tests.

Basis: MedlinePlus: the amount of ALT in the blood isn't related to how much the liver may be damaged; ALT is compared with the other liver tests.

slides.title: Why is ALT considered a more liver-specific marker of damage than AST?
options: ALT is found mostly in the liver, while AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues
ALT is not affected by medicines, exercise or age, so any change in it reflects the liver alone
ALT is released only when liver cancer is present, so a high ALT points to a tumor rather than other damage
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: AST can also rise when tissues outside the liver are damaged, whereas ALT comes mainly from the liver.

Basis: MedlinePlus: ALT is mostly found in the liver and checks more specifically for liver damage; AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues.

slides.title: A patient with no known liver disease has a high AST. Why might the AST come from outside the liver?
options: AST is made only by red blood cells, so any AST in the blood comes from them
AST is also found in the heart, muscles and other tissues and is released when they are damaged
AST rises only when the patient has eaten before the blood draw instead of fasting as instructed
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source also lists non-liver causes of high AST, such as heart problems, deep burns, seizures and surgery.

Basis: MedlinePlus: AST is found mainly in the liver but also in the heart, muscles and other tissues; damaged AST-containing cells release it into the blood.

slides.title: How is a low AST level in the blood usually interpreted?
options: As a sign of liver failure
As proof that the sample was collected incorrectly
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source states that low AST levels in the blood are usually considered normal.

Basis: MedlinePlus: low levels of AST in the blood are usually considered normal.

slides.title: ALP is high, but the other liver tests are normal. Which explanation does the source suggest?
options: A bile duct blockage is confirmed, even though the other liver tests are normal
The only explanation is an error in the laboratory measurement
A bone disorder, such as Paget's disease of bone, may be the cause
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: with high ALP and normal liver tests the problem may be a bone disorder; an ALP isoenzyme test can show the source.

Basis: MedlinePlus: if ALP is high and liver tests are normal, the problem may be a bone disorder such as Paget's disease of bone.

slides.title: A 14-year-old has a high ALP. Which factor from the source should be considered before assuming disease?
options: Children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing
Teens always have very low ALP, so this means liver failure
Age does not affect ALP, so a high value must mean bone or liver disease
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source names bone growth as a reason for high ALP in children and teens.

Basis: MedlinePlus: children and teens may have high ALP because their bones are growing.

Clinical and diagnostic significance of transaminases and methods of determination?
bullets: 1. ALT and AST are enzymes that transfer an amino group from an amino acid to α-ketoglutarate (coenzyme – pyridoxal phosphate, a derivative of vitamin B6).

2. Determination: kinetic UV method (IFCC reference procedure, 37 °C) – the product formed oxidizes NADH in a reaction with an auxiliary enzyme, and the decrease in absorbance at 340 nm is measured; historical colorimetric end-point methods are poorly standardized.
3. ALT is mainly in the liver – more specific for hepatocellular injury; AST in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, erythrocytes.

slides.title: Clinical and diagnostic significance of transaminases and methods of determination?
bullets: 4. Interpretation: very high values – acute viral/toxic/ischemic hepatitis; AST:ALT >2 – alcohol-related injury; isolated AST elevation – muscle (compare with CK) or hemolysis.
5. Preanalytics: hemolysis falsely raises AST; physical exertion, some drugs.

slides.title: The role of the liver in metabolism?
bullets: 1. Carbohydrate metabolism: glycogen synthesis and breakdown, gluconeogenesis – maintaining blood glucose in the fasting state.

2. Protein metabolism: synthesis of albumin, coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X, etc.), transport proteins, acute-phase proteins; transamination of amino acids; conversion of ammonia to urea (ornithine cycle).
3. Lipid metabolism: β-oxidation of fatty acids, synthesis of ketone bodies, synthesis of cholesterol and VLDL, formation of bile acids.
4. Detoxification and excretion: bilirubin conjugation and excretion into bile, metabolism of drugs and toxins, inactivation of hormones; storage of vitamins and iron.

slides.title: The role of the liver in metabolism?
bullets: 5. Laboratory reflection: synthetic function – albumin, PT/INR; damage – ALT, AST; cholestasis – ALP, GGT, bilirubin; in liver failure urea is low, ammonia high, cholinesterase low.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of liver diseases?
bullets: 1. Hepatocellular injury: ALT (more specific for the liver) and AST; AST:ALT >2 – suggests alcohol-related disease; very high aminotransferases – acute viral/toxic/ischemic hepatitis.
2. Cholestasis: disproportionate rise of ALP and GGT, direct bilirubin; R ratio = (ALT/ULN)/(ALP/ULN): >5 hepatocellular, 2–5 mixed, <2 cholestatic pattern.
3. Synthetic function: albumin, PT/INR (reflects function better than enzymes), cholinesterase.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of liver diseases?
bullets: 4. Etiological tests: viral hepatitis (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HCV, HCV RNA and HBV DNA if needed), autoimmune markers, ferritin/iron (hemochromatosis), ceruloplasmin (Wilson disease), alpha-1 antitrypsin.
5. Fibrosis and tumor: noninvasive indices (FIB-4, etc.), AFP (surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma – together with ultrasound).
6. Steatotic liver disease (MASLD) – with cardiometabolic factors; lipid profile, glucose/HbA1c.
